title: Design: tool-calling agent
objective: Split a tool-calling agent into parts (loop, model, tools, memory, guardrail) so each can change and be tested on its own.

sources.title: Anthropic: Building effective agents (agents as models using tools in a loop, with stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations)
Yao et al. (2022), ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

simplifies: The model is an interface here; in tests (and in this app) it's a scripted fake, so there are no live model calls. Real agents also handle tool errors, time limits, cost limits and asking a person for approval.

steps.caption: A first agent is often one big function: call the model, parse its reply, run a tool with an if/elif on its name, append to a list, and stop after N turns.
Split it by job. Agent runs the loop; the Model decides the next step; Tools act; Memory holds history; a Guardrail checks each step.
One turn: the agent sends the history to the model…

predict.prompt: The model asks to call delete_files(). Who should stop it?

options.text: The guardrail, before the tool runs
options.explanation: Right. Checking every step before acting is the guardrail's one job.

options.text: The tool itself, after it has started
options.explanation: By then the damage may be done.
Models make mistakes; tools have real effects.

steps.caption: …and the tool runs. Its result goes back into memory, and the loop goes round again.
Because Model is an interface, a test can pass a scripted FakeModel and check the loop's rules (the turn limit, the guardrail) without any real model calls.

predict.prompt: How do you test that the agent stops after 5 turns, without paying for model calls?

options.text: Pass a FakeModel that never says it's finished, and check the agent stops at 5
options.explanation: Right. The loop's rules are tested on their own.

options.text: Run the real model many times and hope it loops

options.explanation: The loop is ordinary code; only the model needs faking.

exercise.hint: Each of these classes has its own hand-written list of tool names.

options.text: Give every tool a Tool interface (name, description, run) and keep them in one registry that Agent, Prompt and Guardrail read
options.explanation: Right. A new tool is a new class plus one line registering it.

options.text: Add a browse branch to each class's list
options.explanation: Three edits now and for every future tool, and the lists drift apart.

options.text: Let the model call any Python function by name
options.explanation: Then nothing limits what it can run; the guardrail has nothing to check against.

exercise.explain: Agent looks tools up in the registry, Prompt describes the registered tools to the model, and Guardrail checks names against it. Adding browsing is a BrowseTool class plus one line to register it.

quiz.prompt: Why put the model behind a Model interface?

options.text: Tests can swap in a scripted fake, and you can change providers without touching the loop
options.explanation: Right. The loop depends on what a model does, not which one it is.
It's a design choice on your side.
It changes the code's structure, not the model.

quiz.prompt: What should stop an agent that keeps calling the same tool forever?

options.text: A turn limit checked in the loop every turn, with the guardrail as a second line
options.explanation: Right. Stopping conditions belong in the loop's code, not in hope.

options.text: Waiting for the model to notice

options.explanation: That only lets the loop run longer.
